Pigeons are natrually afraid of falcons and hawks since they are the prey and associate the silhouette with bad shit about to go down. But how many generations had to pass before they didnt have to learn to be afraid and were just born that way?
How long before a learned activity becomes instinctual?

I hadn't heard of your example, but I have heard of similar ones. Do you know if pigeons raised in captivity (no exposure to wild pigeons) exhibit this behaviour? The reason I ask is that monkeys raised in the lab don't exhibit a fear of snakes, but when they witness another monkey that is afraid of snakes, they too develop the fear/phobia. Interestingly, if the lab-raised monkey is shown a doctored video of a monkey afraid of flowers (or something equally innocuous), they don't acquire the fear/phobia. This indicates that there is an inherited (genetic) predisposition to acquiring certain phobias - as though the monkeys have an archetype of a snake imprinted somewhere in their brain.

This is one of the ways in which psychology rationalizes why certain phobias (snakes, spiders, darkness, tight spaces, etc.) are disproportionately more common in humans that other phobias - these have been the stimuli that have presented dangers to us over the course of our evolution.. Further evidence of this is that we as humans rarely develop phobias of more recent dangerous inventions (stoves, automobiles, etc.) - those inventions for whose fear we could not have yet evolutionarily selected.

I suspect the same is true in pigeons. A genetic mutation/anomaly in a given pigeon passed to its offspring, caused them to be more fearful of silhouettes. As a result their behaviour differed in the presence of falcons and hawks, and they survived encounters more frequently. By virtue of this, there were more of them to reproduce and the trait spread throughout the species. How long this would take depends on many factors (e.g. how large the population was, how distributed the population was, how strong the environmental pressure was, etc.). Typically, evolutionary traits are said to evolve on the order of millions of years, but most of that time is waiting for the fluke mutation to occur. Realistically, it may have spread in a few generations, or it may have taken hundreds (probably more likely the latter).

It may be worth cross-posting your question to /v/AskScience for more opinions or a more detailed answer.

Edit: I should add, the mutation likely made it instinctual from the start. A learned behaviour can no more become an inherited trait / instinctual, than a missing (severed) arm can be passed on to one's offspring.
